turns.prompt_text: Who invented the ball bearings that I used commonly in like desk chairs and skateboards?
turns.response_html:
The ball bearings found in your desk chair and skateboard don't have a single "Eureka!" moment from one person. Instead, they evolved through several key inventions that took them from crude wooden rollers to the high-precision steel components we use today.

Here are the heavy hitters in the history of the ball bearing:

1. Philip Vaughan (1794): The First Patent

While ancient civilizations (and even Leonardo da Vinci) toyed with the concept of rolling friction, the first modern patent for a ball bearing was granted to Philip Vaughan, a British ironmaster. He designed a system where iron balls supported a carriage axle, though the manufacturing technology of the 18th century wasn't quite ready to make them reliably.

2. Jules Suriray (1869): The Skateboard Ancestor

If you’re looking for the direct ancestor of the bearings in wheels (like skateboards and bicycles), it’s Jules Suriray, a Parisian bicycle mechanic. He patented the first practical radial ball bearing.

Suriray’s bearings were used on the winning bicycle in the world's first major road race, the Paris-Rouen, in 1869. This proved that bearings weren't just a novelty—they were a massive mechanical advantage.

3. Friedrich Fischer (1883): The "Kugelfischer"

Until the late 19th century, ball bearings were difficult to make because the steel balls weren't perfectly round. Friedrich Fischer in Germany invented the Kugelschleifmaschine (ball grinding machine), which could mass-produce steel balls to equal size and high precision. This made bearings affordable and reliable for the first time. His company eventually became FAG, which is still a major bearing manufacturer today.

4. Sven Wingquist (1907): The Self-Aligning Bearing

For things like desk chairs or heavy machinery that might tilt or misalign, Sven Wingquist is the key figure. He was a Swedish engineer who invented the self-aligning ball bearing. This allowed the inner ring to tilt while the outer ring stayed fixed, preventing the bearing from seizing up when things weren't perfectly straight. He went on to found SKF, one of the largest bearing companies in the world.

How they work in your gear:

  • Skateboards: Usually use Deep-Groove Radial Bearings (like Suriray's design). They handle "radial" loads (your weight pushing down) while allowing the wheels to spin at high RPMs.
  • Desk Chairs: Usually use Thrust Bearings or Angular Contact Bearings in the base. These are designed to handle the vertical "thrust" load of you sitting down while still letting you swivel 360° to reach for a snack.

Does that help clear up the history of the "spinny bits" in your life?

turns.prompt_text: A little bit when they become damaged. Like, if you spend them and they have like, grooves in them, is that repairable, in any way.
turns.response_html:
The short answer is: No, not really.

When you see or feel those "grooves" or pits in a bearing, it’s usually game over for that specific part. In the industry, that kind of damage is called spalling or pitting, and it signals the end of the bearing's functional life.

Here is why you generally can't (and shouldn't) try to repair them:

1. The Precision Problem

The balls and the "races" (the tracks they roll in) are manufactured to incredibly tight tolerances—often measured in microns (thousandths of a millimeter). If you were to try and "sand out" a groove or a pit, you would be removing material and changing the geometry of the track. Even a microscopic unevenness will cause the balls to "bounce," creating heat, vibration, and eventually causing the bearing to seize up.

2. Case Hardening

Bearings aren't hard all the way through the same way a rock is. They are often case-hardened, meaning only the outer "skin" of the steel is heat-treated to be ultra-tough. Once a groove wears through that hardened layer into the softer core underneath, the bearing will degrade exponentially faster. Any attempt to grind it down just exposes more of that soft metal.

3. The Cost vs. Risk Factor

  • For Skateboards: A seized bearing at high speed can stop a wheel instantly, which usually results in the rider being launched. Since a decent set of bearings costs $15–$30, the risk isn't worth the reward.
  • For Desk Chairs: You might be able to grease a "crunchy" bearing to buy a few months of time, but once the metal is physically deformed, it will always feel bumpy and eventually drop metal shavings onto your floor.

When is it actually "Repairable"?

There is one caveat: if the bearing feels "gritty" but doesn't actually have physical grooves in the metal, it might just be contaminated.

  • The "Clean and Lube" Strategy: If your bearings have removable shields (common in high-end skate bearings), you can pop the shields off, soak the bearings in a solvent (like isopropyl alcohol) to remove old gunk and sand, and then apply a drop of light synthetic oil.
  • The Verdict: If they still feel "notchy" or "indexed" (like they want to click into certain spots) after a deep clean, the metal itself is deformed.

In the world of massive industrial machinery—think wind turbines or ship engines—specialized companies do "refurbish" bearings by regrinding the races and fitting them with slightly larger oversized balls. But for the "consumer-grade" spinny bits in your life, replacement is the only reliable fix.

Does the "crunchiness" you're feeling happen all the way around the rotation, or just in one specific spot?

turns.prompt_text: I have a few of these ball bearings from the skateboard, I'm taking apart and some of them are very crunchy, some of them just have a spot or two, but you can tell, if, when I flick it by the amount of momentum it carries
turns.response_html:
That "flick test" is a great diagnostic tool. If you flick a bearing and it stops abruptly or feels like it's hitting a "pothole," you’re feeling the physical reality of friction.

Since you've got them out and are feeling those specific "spots," here is how to tell if you’re dealing with a cleaning issue or a permanent metal failure.

1. The "Catch" (Spalling vs. Dirt)

When you feel a specific spot where the bearing "stalls," it’s usually one of two things:

  • Contamination: A tiny grain of sand or metal shard is stuck in the grease. As the ball rolls over it, it creates a temporary speed bump.
  • Spalling (Pitting): This is a permanent "crater" in the steel race. When the ball falls into that crater, it loses its momentum and "clicks."

2. The "Crunchy" Feel (Brinelling)

If the bearing feels like it's rolling over gravel the whole way around, it might be Brinelling. This happens when the bearing takes a heavy side-impact (like a hard landing on the skateboard). The balls actually dent the races.

  • Imagine a smooth road suddenly having permanent, microscopic speed bumps every few inches. You can't clean that away; the metal has been "rearranged."

3. Why Momentum Can Be Deceiving

It’s worth noting that a "dry" bearing (no oil) will often spin for a long time during a flick test, but it will sound loud. A brand-new, high-quality bearing packed with thick factory grease might only spin for a second or two because the grease provides viscous drag.

  • The Goal: You want smoothness, not necessarily the longest spin time. If it spins for 30 seconds but sounds like a jet engine, the metal-on-metal contact is wearing it down fast.

The "Last Ditch" Diagnostic

If you want to see if they are salvageable, you can try a solvent flush:

  1. Remove the Shields: Use a safety pin to pop the rubber or metal shields off.
  2. The Bath: Drop them in a small jar of isopropyl alcohol (90% or higher) or a dedicated bearing cleaner. Shake it up.
  3. The Spin: While they are submerged or wet, spin them. If the "crunch" disappears, it was just dirt. If the "spot" remains in the exact same place every time, the metal race is pitted.
  4. Lube: If they come out smooth, you must add a drop of thin synthetic lubricant (like Bones Speed Cream or even a light machine oil). Running them "dry" after a solvent bath will destroy them in minutes.

If you do the cleaning and that "click" is still there, that bearing is officially a "parts only" item—maybe useful for a low-speed 3D printing project, but not for something you're riding on.

Are the shields on yours the rubberized ones that pop off easily, or the metal ones held in with a tiny C-clip?

Those are classic 608ZZ bearings. The "608" is the size (standard for skateboards), and the "ZZ" tells us they have metal shields on both sides.

Looking at your photo, there is good news: these are the serviceable type. If you look closely at the very outer edge of the silver shield, you can see a tiny, C-shaped wire clipped into a groove. That little wire is what holds the shield in place.

Here is how you can get inside that specific bearing to see if you can fix the "crunch":

1. The C-Clip Removal

You’ll need a very fine point, like a safety pin, a needle, or a dental pick.

  • Find the gap in that tiny C-ring.
  • Pry one end of the ring out of its groove. Be careful—these things like to "ping" across the room and vanish forever.
  • Once the ring is out, the metal shield should just pop right off, exposing the balls and the "cage" holding them.

2. What to Look For Inside

Once it's open, you’ll likely see one of two things:

  • The "Desert": The grease has dried up into a crusty, waxy substance. This is what's causing your "crunchy" feeling. It’s basically rolling over old scabs of oil.
  • The "Gravel Pit": You’ll see actual black specks of grit or sand.

3. The Deep Clean

Since these are metal-shielded, they usually use a thicker grease rather than thin oil. To truly fix that "momentum" issue:

  1. Soak the open bearing in a container of isopropyl alcohol or a degreaser.
  2. Spin it while submerged to work the gunk out.
  3. Dry it completely (a hairdryer or compressed air works great).
  4. Inspect: Give it a dry flick. It should sound loud and tinny, but it should be perfectly smooth. If you still feel that "spot" where it catches, the metal race is physically pitted, and no amount of cleaning will save it.

4. Re-Lubrication

Never run them dry. If the bearing feels smooth after cleaning, add a tiny drop of light machine oil or a dedicated skateboard bearing lubricant. If you want them to last a long time without maintenance, you can pack a little bit of white lithium grease in there, though they won't "flick-spin" as long initially because of the thickness.

Pro-Tip: If you're using these for a skateboard, many people leave the inner shield (the side facing the middle of the wheel) off once they've cleaned them. It makes the next cleaning much easier, as you only have to pop one shield per bearing.

Do you have a needle or a small enough tool to get under that C-clip?

turns.prompt_text: I'm not sure I'm seeing the C clip.
turns.response_html:
It is possible you’re looking at a non-serviceable version. While many 608ZZ bearings use a C-clip, some manufacturers "crimp" or press the metal shield directly into a groove in the outer race to save on production costs.

Here is how to tell the difference and what to look for:

The "Gap" Test

Look at the very outer edge of the silver shield, where it meets the thick outer ring (the race).

  • If it has a clip: You will see a tiny, hair-thin wire tucked into a groove. Most importantly, that wire will have a small gap (about 1–2mm wide) where the two ends of the "C" almost meet.
  • If it is crimped: The metal shield will look like it is tucked under a small lip of the outer race with no visible wire or gap. It will look like one solid, continuous piece of metal all the way around.

How to find it if it's there

These clips are often covered in old grease or "road grime," making them look like part of the bearing.

  1. Clean the edge: Take a paper towel with a bit of isopropyl alcohol and wipe the very outer circumference of the shield thoroughly.
  2. Use a light: Tilt the bearing under a bright desk lamp. You’re looking for a slight reflection from the round wire of the clip versus the flat surface of the shield.
  3. The "Probe": Take a safety pin or a thin sewing needle and run the point along the inside edge of the outer race. If the needle "catches" on a gap, you’ve found the ends of the C-clip.

What if there is no clip?

If you’ve cleaned it and it looks completely smooth with no gap, it’s a permanently shielded bearing.

  • Can you still fix it? Technically, yes, but it's "destructive." You can use a small flathead screwdriver or a pick to pry the metal shield out. However, this usually bends the shield so badly that you can't put it back in.
  • The "Shieldless" Route: Some skaters actually prefer this. They pry the shields off, clean the bearings, and then run them "open" (with no shields). This makes them spin faster and makes cleaning easier, but they will get dirty much faster.

If you're using these for your skateboard, running them open is fine as long as you're okay with cleaning them more often. If you're using them for a 3D printing project or something where they'll be exposed to dust, it's usually better to just replace a crimped bearing once it goes crunchy.

Does the edge look like a smooth, tucked-in lip, or can you see a faint line where a wire might be sitting?

turns.prompt_text: So these are probably as good as they're going to get. I soak them in WD-40 and then rinse them off with water and then dried them.
turns.response_html:
I have to give you a quick "heads-up" on that process—you’ve actually hit the two biggest "taboos" in the bearing world: WD-40 and Water.

While they might feel smoother right this second, you’ve essentially put them on a fast track to seizing up. Here is why, and how to save them before they rust:

1. The Problem with Water

Bearings are made of high-carbon steel. Even if you dried them with a towel, microscopic droplets of water stay trapped in the "races" (the tracks). Within hours, those droplets will cause flash rusting. This creates tiny pits in the metal, which will make the bearing feel crunchier than when you started.

2. The Problem with WD-40

Despite the name, WD-40 is a solvent and water displacer, not a long-term lubricant.

  • It’s great for breaking up old, crusty grease (which you just did).
  • However, it evaporates quickly and leaves behind a very thin, sticky residue that actually attracts dust and dirt.
  • Once it dries, you have metal-on-metal contact. At the high RPMs of a skateboard wheel, that friction will create enough heat to "weld" the balls to the races.

The "Emergency Rescue" Step

If you want these to actually last, you need to do one more thing immediately to get the moisture out and the protection in:

  1. Displace the water: Dip them back into the WD-40 or, even better, 90%+ Isopropyl Alcohol. This will "grab" the water and help it evaporate without leaving rust behind.
  2. Dry with Heat: Use a hairdryer or compressed air to make sure they are bone-dry.
  3. Apply Real Lubricant: This is the non-negotiable part. You need to add a drop or two of synthetic oil (like Bones Speed Cream, 3-in-One oil, or even sewing machine oil).
    • If you don't have oil, a tiny dab of lithium grease or even automotive grease will work, though it will feel "slow" until it warms up.

The Verdict

If you've cleaned them this thoroughly and they still feel crunchy or have "spots," the WD-40 has successfully stripped away the gunk that was hiding the physical damage.

If the crunch is still there when they are clean and dry, the metal is permanently pitted. You can use them for a low-stakes DIY project, but I wouldn't trust them for a downhill skate session!

Do they spin for a long time now, or do they still stop pretty quickly when you flick them?

turns.prompt_text: So, now I wonder where could I Source ball bearings? I imagine going to Goodwill and places that sell things like roller skates and skateboards would help.
turns.response_html:
Sourcing 608zz bearings is actually very easy because they are one of the most common mechanical parts in the world. While thrifting at places like Goodwill is a fun way to "scavenge" (look for old inline skates or fidget spinners), you can also find them brand new for very little money at local hardware and sports stores.

Where to Source Locally

  • Sporting Goods Stores: Places like Dick's Sporting Goods or local skate shops are your best bet for high-quality versions. They will carry brands like Bones Reds, which are the gold standard for skateboards because they are easy to clean.
  • Big Box Retailers: Target and Walmart usually stock replacement 608zz bearings in their sports/skateboarding section. You can often find a 4-pack or 8-pack for under $10.
  • Hardware & Industrial Stores: Since you are in the Ames and Ankeny area, you have access to industrial suppliers like ABC Supply or even general hardware stores like Menards or Home Depot. They often stock them for use in power tools and small electric motors.

Common Household "Donors"

If you want to scavenge them from items you might already have or find at a thrift store, look for:

  • Inline Skates/Rollerblades: These usually contain 16 bearings (two per wheel). Even a beat-up pair from Goodwill for $5 can be a "gold mine" of 608 bearings.
  • Fidget Spinners: Almost every standard fidget spinner uses a 608 bearing as its center weight or main spinner.
  • Power Tools: Some older sanders and drills use 608 bearings for the motor shaft.
  • Vacuum Cleaners: The brush rollers in many upright vacuums use these bearings (though they are often very dirty).

Recommended Replacement Options

If your current "crunchy" bearings are too far gone, here are a few highly-rated options you can pick up.

Top Choice for Skateboarding

The Bones Reds Bearings are widely considered the best "bang for your buck." They are skate-rated, meaning they handle the side-loads of turning better than industrial bearings. They also feature a single, non-contact rubber shield that makes them significantly easier to clean than the metal-shielded ones you have now.

High-Performance Option

If you want something that can handle a bit more "abuse" (like the moisture from your recent cleaning), BONES Ceramic Super Reds use ceramic balls that do not rust. While the outer steel rings can still rust, the ceramic balls will actually "self-clean" by crushing small bits of grit that get inside.

Budget Industrial Options

If you just need a lot of bearings for a DIY project and don't care about "pro" skate performance, you can buy them in bulk.

  • Naive Blue 608 ZZ Ball Bearings (10 Pack): A very affordable set of standard double-shielded bearings.
  • NSK Deep Groove Ball Bearing 608ZZ: A higher-precision industrial bearing that is very quiet and reliable.

Since you've already tried the WD-40 and water method, would you like me to look for a specific local shop in Ames that has Bones Reds in stock today so you can get back on your board?

turns.prompt_text: One thing I wonder it looks like at least in the skateboard. The inner and outer circles were connected via friction and nothing else.
turns.response_html:
It’s a common misconception that they’re just "stuck" together, but it’s actually a clever bit of geometry rather than friction. If you’ve ever tried to pull the inner circle (the inner race) out of the outer circle (outer race), you’ve probably noticed it won't budge.

Here is the "mechanical magic" behind how those pieces stay joined:

1. The Groove Geometry

Both the inner and outer races have deep, curved channels called grooves. The steel balls sit inside these grooves. Because the "lips" of these grooves are slightly narrower than the diameter of the balls, the balls are physically trapped. They can’t move left or right, which in turn keeps the inner race locked centered inside the outer race.

2. The Retainer (or Cage)

If you were to remove the shields and look inside, you’d see a plastic or metal "comb" holding the balls apart. This is the cage. Without it, the balls would all bunch up on one side, and the inner race would simply fall out the other side. The cage ensures the balls are distributed evenly around the circle, maintaining the structural integrity of the "sandwich."

3. The Assembly "Secret"

You might wonder: If they are trapped, how do they get them in there in the first place?

  • Manufacturers use an eccentric assembly method.
  • They push the inner race all the way to one side, creating a large gap on the opposite side.
  • They drop the balls into that gap.
  • Then, they center the inner race and snap the cage into place to lock the balls into their final positions.

Where to Source Replacements Locally

If you're looking for fresh bearings around Ames or Ankeny without waiting for shipping, you have a few solid options:

  • Subculture Skateboards (Ames): Located on Main Street, this is your best bet for high-quality "Skate Rated" bearings like Bones Reds. They’ll have exactly what you need and can often help you press them into your wheels if you don't have a dedicated tool.
  • Standard Bearings (Urbandale/Des Moines): If you just need "bulk" industrial 608zz bearings for a 3D printing project or a desk chair, these guys are pros. They carry standard sizes in higher quantities than a typical hardware store.
  • Dunham’s Sports (Ames): Located in the North Grand Mall, they usually carry basic replacement sets for skateboards and inline skates.

Recommended Bearings

For your skateboard, I'd suggest sticking with "skate-rated" options. They are built to handle the "side-loading" (lateral force) that happens when you turn, which standard industrial bearings aren't always designed for.

The Bones Reds are the standard choice for a reason. They use a removable rubber shield instead of the metal ones you currently have. This makes cleaning them (properly, without water!) significantly easier in the future.

If you want a step up, Bones Super Reds use higher-grade steel and a finer surface finish, which provides a smoother roll and better momentum for the "flick test" you were doing.

turns.prompt_text: What I mean, is the connection between the outer wheel. And the skateboard wheel is just held there by friction and the connection of the inner bearing wheel to the axle of the skateboard is also just friction.
turns.response_html:
You hit the nail on the head regarding the wheel, but the axle connection is actually doing something much more "industrial" than just relying on friction.

Here is the breakdown of how those connections actually work:

1. Bearing to Wheel: The "Press Fit"

You are exactly right here. This is called an Interference Fit (or Press Fit). The bearing is physically a tiny bit larger than the hole in the urethane wheel.

  • How it holds: The plastic of the wheel stretches slightly as the bearing is pushed in, creating constant tension that grips the outer ring of the bearing.
  • The friction factor: This friction is vital because if the outer ring slipped inside the wheel, it would melt the plastic from the heat.

2. Bearing to Axle: The "Slip Fit" & Clamping Force

This is where it gets interesting. The connection between the inner ring and the axle is actually a Slip Fit (or Clearance Fit). The hole in the bearing is slightly larger than the axle so it can slide on easily.

  • It’s not friction: If you only relied on friction here, the inner ring would eventually spin on the axle and grind it down (a phenomenon called "creep").
  • It’s Clamping: On a properly set up board, the axle nut is the hero. When you tighten it, you are actually "sandwiching" or clamping the inner rings together.

The "Missing Links": Spacers and Speed Rings

If your bearings feel like they lose momentum when you tighten the nut, it’s usually because two tiny (but critical) parts are missing:

  • Bearing Spacers: This is a small metal tube that sits inside the wheel between the two bearings. It allows you to tighten the axle nut all the way down without crushing the bearing's internal parts. It locks the inner races together so they become one solid "sleeve" on the axle.
  • Speed Rings (Washers): These tiny washers sit on either side of the bearings. They ensure the axle nut and the truck's "shoulder" only touch the inner race. Without them, the nut might rub against the shield or outer race, creating the "crunchy" friction you're feeling.

Why this matters for your "Crunchy" Bearings:

If you don't use spacers, tightening the nut puts lateral (side) pressure on the balls inside. This can actually cause those "grooves" or pits we talked about earlier.

Pro-Tip for your Ames/Ankeny Setup: Since you're already doing DIY hardware work, you might find that using a dedicated Skate Tool (which has the specific deep-well sockets for axles and kingpins) is way easier than using a standard wrench set. You can usually grab a "T-Tool" and a set of spacers at Subculture on Main Street in Ames for about the price of a sandwich.

turns.prompt_text: I wonder if I can make a 3D print using these bearings. I would probably need for the. I'm not sure exactly how I would do it though.
turns.response_html:
Since you've got those 608ZZ bearings out and cleaned, they are perfect for a variety of functional 3D printing projects. They are essentially the "building blocks" of movement in the maker world.

Given their 8mm inner diameter, 22mm outer diameter, and 7mm width, here is how you can integrate them into your next design.

1. Top Project Ideas for 608ZZ Bearings

  • Filament Spool Rollers: This is the most common use. You can print a "side-car" roller or a dry-box mount. Using bearings makes the pull from the extruder much smoother, reducing tension and improving print quality.
  • Rotating Display Base: If you’re working on something like an air quality monitor or a small electronics housing, a bearing-supported base allows the device to swivel 360° for easy access to ports.
  • Fidget Gear Systems: Since you’re already testing their "flick" momentum, building a planetary gear set or a simple hand spinner is a great way to use the ones that are still smooth.
  • Bearing Cleaning Spinner: You can actually 3D print a small "drill attachment" that holds a bearing securely. This allows you to spin the bearing at high speeds using a power drill during the cleaning process to centrifugal out all the old WD-40 or gunk.

2. The Technical "How-To" for CAD

When designing a part to hold a bearing, you shouldn't just draw a 22mm hole. 3D printers often "squish" the filament, making holes slightly smaller than the digital model.

  • The Tolerance Secret: For a standard Press Fit (where the bearing stays in by friction), design your hole at 22.1mm or 22.2mm. This usually accounts for the "elephant's foot" or slight over-extrusion, allowing you to push the bearing in by hand with a satisfying "pop."
  • Designing a "Shoulder": You don't want the bearing to slide all the way through the hole. Design a small 1mm internal lip (a shoulder) at the bottom of the hole. This gives the outer race something to rest against while leaving the inner race free to spin.
  • The Shaft: For the center axle, a 7.8mm or 7.9mm cylinder usually slides through an 8mm bearing hole perfectly without being loose.

3. Material and Nozzle Tips

  • Rigid vs. Flexible: If you use a rigid material like PLA or PETG, your tolerances need to be exact. However, if you use a 90A TPU, you can design the hole at exactly 22mm. The "give" in the rubbery filament will grip the bearing like a glove and help dampen any "crunchy" vibrations or noise.
  • Layer Heights: Using a 0.6mm nozzle is great for speed, but for bearing seats, try to keep your layer height around 0.2mm or 0.24mm. Thinner layers make for a smoother "wall" inside the hole, which provides a more even grip on the bearing.

Replacement Options

If you find that your scavenged bearings are just too far gone (or if the "crunch" drives you crazy), you can pick up a fresh set of high-quality replacements. The Bones Reds are the gold standard for anything that needs to spin fast and stay clean.

If you want to go all-in on a project and don't want to worry about rust, Ceramic Bearings are a great choice, especially for anything involving moisture or outdoor use.
